articles.title: Auto-detecting file types taught me guesses need an escape hatch
articles.excerpt: I shipped a single endpoint that takes any document and returns Markdown, and the first week was mostly about the bytes before the conversion. PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, EPUB, HTML — none of them announce…
articles.body: I shipped a single endpoint that takes any document and returns Markdown, and the first week was mostly about the bytes before the conversion. PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, EPUB, HTML — none of them announce themselves reliably. Magic numbers lie, extensions lie more, and a PDF renamed .txt is still a PDF. The lesson I keep returning to: when you auto-detect, you are making a guess on behalf of the caller, so the guess has to be inspectable. I added a detected_type field to the response and a way to force the parser when the guess is wrong. That turned silent corruption into a boring error the agent can correct on the next call. Most "bad output" reports weren't converter bugs; they were wrong sniffing. The second lesson is that one door only works if the door tells you what went through it.

articles.title: Apache APISIX Admin Exposure: The Gap Between a 9180 Listener and a Key-Protected Control Plane
articles.excerpt: Apache APISIX Admin Exposure: The Gap Between a 9180 Listener and a Key-Protected Control Plane Apache APISIX uses its Admin API to change routes, upstreams, consumers, and other gateway configuration…
articles.body: Apache APISIX Admin Exposure: The Gap Between a 9180 Listener and a Key-Protected Control Plane Apache APISIX uses its Admin API to change routes, upstreams, consumers, and other gateway configuration. The official documentation shows the Admin API on port 9180 and uses an X-API-KEY header for administrative requests. That makes the control plane an attractive asset to inventory. A public listener is not proof that the API is unauthenticated, and a missing key in a scan is not proof that the service is vulnerable. The useful question is how many assets can be associated with APISIX, and which of those associations are strong enough to inspect. On November 8, 2026, ZoomEye count-only queries for this assessment used sub_type=all , page 1, and page size 1.

articles.title: AI Ships Fast, but Focus Drifts
articles.excerpt: One incident still sticks with me. Our application services have to update a batch of data in shared memory atomically. That memory is managed centrally by the system: cross-process locks, memory orde…
articles.body: One incident still sticks with me. Our application services have to update a batch of data in shared memory atomically. That memory is managed centrally by the system: cross-process locks, memory ordering, and version switching are all wrapped inside the .so library, and callers reach it through a single shared header. At the time, though, the library offered no interface for "atomic bulk update". The AI's approach was about as blunt as it gets: grab the physical address through mmap , overwrite field by field according to its own reading of the layout, and casually invent a flag on the side to serve as a "currently being modified" lock. In a single process it ran fine, and the tests passed.

articles.title: Why coding agent memory files go stale - and what teams should do instead

articles.body: Originally published at getlockstep.dev . A coding agent reads a memory file that says the checkout migration is blocked on database approval. The approval landed last week. The migration shipped. The task closed. Nobody removed the note. The agent now plans around a blocker that no longer exists. This failure is easy to misdiagnose as weak retrieval. The agent retrieved the exact memory the team gave it. The problem is lifecycle: temporary state survived without an owner, status, or expiry, so old context still looked current.

articles.title: AI Agent Memory: Anthropic's 4 Layers, Built in Python

articles.body: Agent memory is the record of what an AI agent learned in past sessions, kept as text it can load again later. Anthropic measured what that record is worth on 6 November 2026: with memory, Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.838 on the company's Continual Learning Bench, up from 0.655 without it. We build a working version in Python below. Key takeaways Anthropic splits agent memory into four layers: transcripts, notes, representations such as wikis, and a small block of injected context. Memory lifted every recent Claude model on CL-Bench. Older models gained most: Opus 4.7 rose from 0.383 to 0.700. Offline "dreaming" passes fix wrong notes. In a Pokémon Red run, a corrected note let the agent reach Cerulean City, which the wrong note had blocked.

articles.title: Postman Is a Desktop App: Testing APIs When You're Not at Your Desk
articles.excerpt: It's 11pm. Production is returning 502s on one endpoint and only one, and the person who noticed is asking you to confirm whether it's still happening. You are not at your laptop. This sounds like a s…
articles.body: It's 11pm. Production is returning 502s on one endpoint and only one, and the person who noticed is asking you to confirm whether it's still happening. You are not at your laptop. This sounds like a small problem. It isn't, because every option you have at 11pm is bad in a different way. Termux and curl. Works fine. Becomes miserable the moment you need an auth header, a request body, or the same environment variables you used yesterday. Wait until morning. Correct, and completely useless to the person currently waiting on you. A cloud request tunnel. Sends production traffic and its auth headers through a third party's logs. I've done it. I don't love it. A public API playground. Requires pasting an internal URL and a bearer token into someone else's website.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.

articles.title: 'I think we will prevail': NASA chief Jared Isaacman on Artemis, China and the new moon race (exclusive)
articles.excerpt: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during a a Dec. 3, 2025 confirmation hearing. In October of 2026, Isaacman sat down with Space.com to discuss the future of the space agency.
articles.body: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition. "I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com. We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program , and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
